newsitem.title: UK: UK's Oftel ready to discuss BT school plan.
newsitem.headline: UK's Oftel ready to discuss BT school plan.

text.p: Telecoms watchdog Oftel said on Wednesday it had its own ideas on how British Telecommunications Plc should offer cheap Internet computer access to schools, although it welcomed a long-term proposal by the UK phone giant.

"(BT's proposal) seems to offer a good way forward but it raises some big issues that will have a major impact on all sectors of the telecoms market, including Internet service providers -- and we must consult and get their views on it," a spokesman for Oftel said.
"We also have some ideas of our own," he added, declining to give details.
Oftel has already rejected BT's temporary plans to offer Internet access to schools in time for the beginning of the academic year in Autumn.
Director general Don Cruickshank said the plan was anti-competitive because it only offered Internet access via a small number of mainly BT-owned service providers using its network.

But the watchdog, which said it would put its own proposals as well as those from BT on the table for an open discussion at the beginning of July, added it hoped BT would be able to offer schools the service as early into the academic year as possible.

"We have agreed to move forward in a spirit of partnership so that the telecoms industry as a whole can make a contribution to the government's widely supported objective," Cruickshank said in an open letter to BT's chief executive Peter Bonfield.

At issue are interconnection payments, which BT pays other operators for carrying a call to one of the many on-line service provider on their networks. This charge affects BT's ability to offer schools affordable prices that are not below cost.
A BT spokeswoman said that BT would not want to deliver calls below cost and said interconnect charges might have to fall.

The Labour government has been keen for schools, hospitals and libraries to be hooked up to the Internet and has said that in exchange, it would consider ending early a ban on BT broadcasting potentially lucrative entertainment services down its telephone lines.

Oftel has been at pains to insist that the two issues are unrelated. But the spokeswoman for BT, which sees few profits from a school deal but points to the growth potential for computer-versed children wanting computers at home, added:
"It's a step towards delivering what schools want. We will obviously still talk to the government about the restrictions (on entertainment) -- and we would seek to have those restrictions lifted."
Meanwhile, Oftel has already approved cable company plans to give schools access to the Internet and some 600-800 have signed up under the scheme.
However, only BT, with its nation-wide coverage, can help the government realise its plans to have all 24,000 schools linked up to the "information superhighway".
Cable companies' prices are broadly similar to those offered by BT -- one pound per pupil per school, Oftel has said.
